t: Serving the Lord, or serving the time?
p: A few Western manuscripts read 'serving the time' instead of 'serving the Lord'.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles and the Byzantine text; the KJV ('serving the Lord')

Codex Claromontanus (D, 500s), Augiensis (F) and Boernerianus (G) in their first hands and some Old Latin copies (as reported by Metzger; manuscript lists not checked here). The STEPBible word list also marks the Textus Receptus with 'the time', although the KJV renders 'the Lord', so printed Textus Receptus editions seem to differ

why: The Lord is the reading of every critical edition and the Byzantine text, and it fits Paul's usual language. 'The time' looks like a copyist's slip (the two words differ by a few letters, and both were abbreviated in manuscripts) or a wish to say 'make the best of your chances'. Origen's commentary (in Rufinus' Latin) mentions copies with 'serving the time', which shows the reading was in circulation early.
b: Kyrios and kairos could be abbreviated in ways that look alike in Greek manuscripts. Rufinus' Latin of Origen mentions copies that read tempori servientes, 'serving the time'.

t: Needs of the saints, or memorials of the saints?

why: 'Needs' fits the next line about hospitality and the collection (15:26). 'Memorials' (mneiais) is one letter different from chreiais and probably arose from a copyist's slip in the Western tradition; some later readers took it to mean the remembrance of martyrs.

p: The accent decides between a woman's name and a man's: Junia or Junias.

readings.w: SBLGNT, NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles, Textus Receptus and Byzantine text (Ἰουνίαν, a woman); the Greek and Latin fathers who comment, e.g. Chrysostom
NA26 (1979), and some English versions that followed it, such as the RSV (Ἰουνιᾶν, a man's name, 'Junias')

why: The earliest manuscripts have no accents, so the name was read by the reader. 'Junia' is a common Roman woman's name; 'Junias' as a man's name is not found in ancient inscriptions (Epp), and the Greek fathers took her as a woman. A male Junias appears in late lists and then in the Middle Ages. See the note and the card.
b: This is a question of reading and accent, not of different manuscripts. Both forms are accusative: Iounian is Junia (accented on the second syllable) and Iounian with a circumflex is Junias.

p: The closing doxology (16:25-27) stands at five different places in the manuscripts, and is missing from a few; see the deep dive.

readings.w: After 16:23, at the end of the letter: NA28, Tyndale House, Westcott-Hort, Tregelles and the Textus Receptus (the STEPBible table does not mark the SBLGNT at 16:25-27); Sinaiticus (01), Vaticanus (03), Ephraemi (04) and Claromontanus (06) are reported to place it here (as reported by NA28 and Metzger; not checked against images)

readings.w: After 14:23: the Byzantine majority text, with manuscripts such as L and Psi (as reported by Metzger); Origen knew copies of this kind. The Textus Receptus (KJV) prints it at the end, as the critical text does
After 15:33: Papyrus 46 (about AD 200)
Omitted: Boernerianus (G) and Augiensis (F) are reported to leave it out; Marcion's text, according to Origen, lacked it with the rest of the letter after 14:23

why: It stands at the end in the great uncials of the critical text and in the Latin Vulgate, and these are the earliest complete copies. The doxology is old, and its movement makes sense if copies of Romans circulated in a form that ended at 14:23 or at 15:33; Paul's authorship is debated (see the deep dive). The Plain English Translation translates it where NA28 and Tyndale House print it, after 16:23.
b: Alexandrinus (02) and a few others have it twice, after 14:23 and again at the end. The three verses go together: see also 16:26 and 16:27, and the entries at 14:23 and 15:33. The final line of many Byzantine and Textus Receptus copies, 'To the Romans, written from Corinth by Phoebe, servant of the church at Cenchreae', is a subscription added by scribes and is not Paul's.
